identification.summary: Taffeta Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-based espionage actor that Microsoft's public naming mapping equates with TURBINE PANDA (CrowdStrike), APT26, TECHNETIUM, TG-0055, Red Kobold, JerseyMikes and BEARCLAW [S1]. CrowdStrike describes Turbine Panda as a China-linked group that targeted aerospace, defense and manufacturing entities, with reporting centred on suppliers to China's C919 airliner [S2][S3][S9]. Google lists APT26 as targeting aerospace, defense and energy for intellectual property theft [S8].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike reporting links the intrusion activity to roughly 2010-2015, starting after COMAC chose CFM International as C919 engine supplier [S2][S3]. CrowdStrike's adversary page says it tracks attacks 'primarily beginning in 2014' [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft's mapping lists only names, not a Microsoft narrative profile; no Microsoft-authored report on Taffeta Typhoon was found [S1]. Vendor cluster boundaries differ: the Turbine Panda / JSSD narrative comes from CrowdStrike (via secondary press) [S2][S3], while APT26 malware lists come from Google [S8]. Do not merge the two without checking. The mapping equates the names, but each vendor's underlying evidence set may differ.

attribution.sponsor: CrowdStrike, as reported by Security Affairs and others, ties Turbine Panda operations to the Jiangsu Bureau of the Ministry of State Security (JSSD) of the People's Republic of China [S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: This is CrowdStrike's assessment as relayed by press coverage; the original CrowdStrike blog was not retrievable here. CrowdStrike also reportedly regards the Sakula malware as unique to Turbine Panda and JSSD [S2][S9]. No government attribution to Taffeta Typhoon by name was found.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike reporting says JSSD officers recruited insiders at foreign aviation firms while cyber operators ran intrusions in parallel [S3][S2]. US prosecutions of JSSD officer Xu Yanjun and associated hackers are cited by the press as related to this operation [S3][S6]. Malware overlap (Sakula, PlugX, Winnti) is cited as technical basis [S4].

objectives: Theft of aerospace intellectual property to help close technology gaps in components for the Chinese C919 airliner and its engine program, per CrowdStrike reporting [S3][S5]; Google summarizes APT26 as IP theft against aerospace, defense and energy [S8].

regions: United States and Europe (aerospace suppliers such as GE, Honeywell, Safran) [S4][S6]
targeting.notes: Named C919 supplier victims in press coverage of CrowdStrike's report include Safran, Capstone Turbine, Ametek, Honeywell and GE [S4]. DOJ's 2018 case against Xu Yanjun describes attempts to obtain GE Aviation composite fan module technology and a Safran laptop infection, as reported by AIN and WCPO [S6]. Whether those cases are the same cluster as Taffeta Typhoon rests on CrowdStrike's linkage in press coverage [S3].

capabilities.summary: CrowdStrike reportedly states Turbine Panda used the Sakula RAT, which it considers unique to the group and JSSD, plus PlugX and Winnti-family tools shared with other Chinese groups [S2][S4]. CrowdStrike's adversary page notes heavy use of PlugX [S9]. Google's APT26 page lists SOGU, HTRAN, POSTSIZE, TWOCHAINS and BEACON [S8]. Operations combined human sources (insider recruitment) with cyber intrusion [S3][S2].

campaigns.name: C919 supply-chain espionage
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reports intrusions against companies supplying C919 components, beginning around the COMAC-CFM engine selection, with JSSD directing human and cyber collection.

campaigns.name: Safran and GE Aviation targeting (Xu Yanjun case)
campaigns.summary: Press reporting on DOJ indictments describes malware planted via an insider on a Safran employee's computer in 2013-2014 and an attempt to obtain GE Aviation fan-module data; Xu was arrested in April 2018. The link of this case to Taffeta Typhoon comes from CrowdStrike's JSSD narrative.

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike publishes Turbine Panda report
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike publicly links Turbine Panda and JSSD to a decade-long effort supporting C919 development.

diamond.adversary: Operators assessed by CrowdStrike to be tied to the Jiangsu MSS bureau, with insiders recruited at victim firms [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Sakula, PlugX, Winnti-family malware plus HUMINT-enabled access [S2][S4]; Google lists SOGU, HTRAN, POSTSIZE, TWOCHAINS, BEACON [S8].
diamond.victim: Aerospace component suppliers and engine makers (GE, Honeywell, Safran and others) [S4][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: State industrial-development goal of narrowing technology gaps for the C919 and its engine [S3][S5].
diamond.technology: Commercial aerospace design and manufacturing data held on corporate networks and on insider-accessible systems [S3][S6].

gaps: No Microsoft-authored threat profile for Taffeta Typhoon was found; Microsoft's mapping gives alias equivalence only [S1].

The original CrowdStrike Turbine Panda blog, the Mandiant APT26 report, Secureworks BRONZE EXPRESS profile, USCC testimony and FireEye 2019 summit slides could not be opened (host fetch failures); claims rely on press coverage and search snippets.
Most public detail is from 2010-2019; recent (2024-2026) Taffeta Typhoon activity was not found.
Whether the Xu Yanjun / Safran DOJ cases correspond to this exact cluster is CrowdStrike's judgment as relayed by press; DOJ filings were not reviewed.
Infrastructure details (domains, IPs, hosting) were not found.
Google's APT26 malware list (SOGU, HTRAN, etc.) differs from CrowdStrike's Sakula emphasis; the overlap is unresolved [S8][S2].
A 2019 FireEye summit presentation referenced in the record was not read; its content is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the defense-aerospace industrial base: engine, avionics and composite-component suppliers and their design and engineering networks, plus overseas offices and personnel visiting China [S3][S6]. STEP 2: The actor combines insider recruitment with malware, so technical controls alone do not close the problem [S3]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is a RAT (Sakula, PlugX, Winnti-family) on engineering hosts, document collection and exfiltration [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet IP theft against aerospace and defense suppliers aligned to Chinese programs. MDCOA is targeting of DoD aircraft-engine or sustainment suppliers to support military rather than civil programs; this extension is not shown in the sources. Candidate indicators: PlugX or Sakula artifacts on engineering workstations, unusual copying of CAD or composite design files, and travel-linked device infections [S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track contractor-reported intrusions in aerospace supply chains and maintain alias mapping (Taffeta Typhoon / Turbine Panda / APT26) so reports from different vendors are correlated [S1]. (2) Authorities: DIB contractor networks fall under DC3/DIB-CS and company authorities, not DAF-owned terrain; coordinate through those channels. (3) Mission assurance: protect weapon-system sustainment and engine data held by suppliers. (4) Coordination: counterintelligence and insider-threat programs must be linked, because the reported tradecraft uses recruited insiders [S3].
